title: Space Tech Briefing — September 28, 2026
summary:
Good morning, space enthusiasts! It's September 28, 2026, and you're tuned into the Space Technology Morning Briefing, your daily dose of cosmic innovation and exploration! We've got some incredible updates from across our solar system today, including a crucial maneuver for a Jupiter-bound explorer and a fascinating look back at a groundbreaking lunar discovery.

First up, some breaking news from our own backyard! The European Space Agency's JUICE probe, on its epic journey to Jupiter, has just completed another vital Earth flyby! This isn't just a pretty picture opportunity; JUICE is using our planet's gravitational pull to precisely refine its trajectory. It's all part of the intricate dance to ensure a safe and successful arrival at the gas giant in 2031. And here's the exciting part for scientists: during this close approach, JUICE's instruments were powered up for scientific purposes, gathering invaluable data even before its main mission truly begins at Jupiter. What an incredible way to leverage these planetary slingshots!

And as we wait for today's new launches and future deep-space events, let's take a moment to look back at a major recent development that captivated the lunar science community. Just a few days ago, we heard about the discovery of the largest impact crater on the Moon in over a century! Using high-resolution images from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, scientists pinpointed this massive new feature. It's a colossal 222 meters in diameter, plunging about 43 meters deep, and surrounded by an astonishing 7-kilometer-wide "cold spot" – a thermal signature of the impact. This monumental crater formed relatively recently, between April 11th and May 22nd, 2024, when an asteroid or comet, estimated to be the size of a 3 to 6-story building, slammed into the lunar surface. It's been officially named in honor of the late American scientist Tom McGetchin, a geologist and planetary scientist renowned for his work on impact craters. A fitting tribute to a pioneer in the field!

What a morning for space exploration! From gravity assists to lunar scars, our universe continues to surprise and inspire. That's all for your Space Technology Morning Briefing today, September 28, 2026. Keep looking up, stay curious, and we'll catch you next time with more thrilling updates from beyond our world. Have a fantastic day!
